source_text:
Sed fortasse dicatis illa mala de talibus naturis non posse auferri et ideo naturalia debere accipi. non nunc quaeritur, quid possit uel non possit auferri, sed certe non paruum lumen est ad intellegendum omnes naturas, in quantum naturae sunt. bonas esse, quod sine illis malis cogitari bona illa possunt, sine bonis autem illis nulla natura cogitari potest. nam sine turbatione caeni possum aquas cogitare, sine pace autem continuatarum partium nulla species corporis animo occurrit, aut ullo modo sentiri potest. ac per hoc nec illae caenosae aquae sine isto bono esse potuerunt, quo bono fiebat, ut aliqua natura corporea posset esse. nam quod dicitis, quod illa mala de naturis talibus non possunt auferri, respondetur, quod et illa bona de naturis talibus non possunt auferri. cur ergo istas res propter mala, quae auferri non posse arbitramini, mala naturalia uocare uultis, propter ea bona uero, quae auferri non posse conuincimini, bona naturalia uocare non uultis?
Restat, ut quaeratis — nam ipsa solet esse uox ultima — unde sint illa mala, quae mihi quoque displicere dicebam. respondebo fortasse. si uos prius dixeritis, unde sint illa bona, quae uos quoque laudare cogimini, si absurdissimi cordis esse non uultis. sed quid ego istud quaeram, cum utrique fateamur omnia, quaecumque et quantacumque bona sunt, ab uno esse deo, qui summe bonus est ? resistite ergo uos ipsi Manichaeo, qui tot et tanta bona, quae commemorauimus iusteque laudauimus, pacem concordiamque partium in unaquaque natura, salutem ualentiamque animantium et cetera, quae repetere iam piget, ita in terra conmenticia tenebrarum esse arbitratus est, ut ab illo deo, quem bonorum omnium fatetur auctorem, alienare conaretur. non enim ea bona uidit, dum hoc solum adtendit, quod displiceret, tamquam si quispiam leonis fremitu exterritus et eum intuens trahentem ac dilaniantem pecorum aut hominum corpora, quaecumque adprehendisset, puerili quadam infirmitate animi tanto timore percelleretur, ut solam feritatem leonis intuens atque saeuitiam, cetera eius neglegens omnino atque praeteriens naturam illius animantis non tantum malum, sed magnum malum esse clamaret, tanto scilicet exaggeratius, quanto timidius; at si edomita feritate duci leonem mansuetum uideret, praesertim si numquam antea fuisset de illa bestia territus, tunc uacaret securo atque intrepido leonis pulchritudinem considerare atque laudare. de quo ego nihil dicam, nisi quod ad rem maxime pertinet, fieri posse, ut aliqua natura offendat ex aliquo et in totam nascatur odium, cum manifestum sit multo meliorem esse speciem uerae ac uiuae bestiae, etiam cum terret in siluis, quam imitatae atque simulatae, cum in pariete picta laudatur. hoc ergo errore ille nos non decipiat nec caecos faciat ad considerandas naturarum species, cum quaedam in eis ita reprehendit, ut omni ex parte cogat displicere, quod omni ex parte reprehendere non potest. atque hoc modo animum ad aequum iudicium conponentes quaeramus iam, unde sint cum illis bonis mala, quae me quoque inprobare dicebam. quod facilius uidebimus, si in unum nomen potuerimus cuncta conferre.
thought_title: Goods inseparable from natures, and the error of hating a whole nature
orientation: Augustine is answering the imagined Manichaean objection that the evils in certain natures cannot be removed, and is about to ask where evil comes from.
pass_a_gloss: But perhaps you may say that those evils cannot be removed from such natures and therefore they must be accepted as natural. It is not now asked what can or cannot be removed, but certainly it is no small light for understanding that all natures, insofar as they are natures, are good, because those good things can be thought without those evils, but without those good things no nature can be thought. For without the disturbance of mud I can think waters, but without the peace of parts joined together no form of a body occurs to the mind, or can be perceived in any way. And through this not even those muddy waters could have existed without this good, by which good it came about that some corporeal nature could exist. For what you say, that those evils cannot be removed from such natures, it is answered that those good things also cannot be removed from such natures. Why therefore do you wish to call these things natural evils because of the evils which you judge cannot be removed, but because of those good things which you are proven cannot be removed you do not wish to call them natural goods? It remains that you ask—for this is usually the last word—where those evils come from, which I was saying displease me too. I will answer perhaps, if you first say where those good things come from, which you too are compelled to praise, if you do not wish to be of the most absurd heart. But why should I ask this, when both of us confess that all things, whatever and however great goods they are, are from the one God, who is supremely good? Therefore resist Mani yourselves, who judged that so many and such great goods, which we have mentioned and rightly praised—the peace and concord of parts in each nature, the health and strength of living things, and the rest, which it is now tedious to repeat—are in the fictitious land of darkness in such a way that he tried to alienate them from that God, whom he confesses to be the author of all goods. For he did not see those goods, while he attended only to this, what displeased him, just as if someone terrified by the roar of a lion and looking at it dragging and tearing apart the bodies of cattle or men, whatever it had seized, should be struck with such great fear by a certain childish weakness of mind that, looking only at the ferocity and savagery of the lion, neglecting and passing over all its other qualities entirely, he should cry out that the nature of that animal is not only an evil but a great evil, all the more exaggeratedly, of course, the more timidly; but if with its ferocity tamed he should see a gentle lion being led, especially if he had never before been terrified of that beast, then he would have leisure to consider and praise the beauty of the lion with security and without fear. About which I will say nothing except what pertains most to the matter, that it can happen that some nature offends from some aspect and hatred is born against the whole, although it is manifest that the form of a true and living beast is much better, even when it terrifies in the woods, than of an imitated and counterfeit one, when it is praised painted on a wall. Therefore let him not deceive us by this error nor make us blind to considering the forms of natures, when he reprehends certain things in them in such a way that he forces to displease what he cannot reprehend in every part. And composing our mind to fair judgment in this way, let us now ask where the evils together with those goods come from, which I was saying I too disapprove. Which we will see more easily if we can bring all things together into one name.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'land of darkness' for terra tenebrarum; 'conmenticia' means invented or fictitious, which Augustine uses to deny its reality.
The glossary requires 'form' for species; here it is the form of a physical body.
The glossary requires 'nature' for natura; the plural is used throughout for created kinds.
The contrast is between goods and evils that are said to be natural; 'natural' is the standard rendering of naturalia.
rejected: goods of nature / evils of nature

choices.why: The glossary bans 'being' for substantia but not for bonus; 'supremely good' renders the superlative of bonus.

choices.english: by a certain childish weakness of mind
choices.why: The phrase describes the irrational fear that leads to hating a whole nature; 'childish weakness of mind' keeps the literal sense.

pass_b_english: But perhaps you will say that those evils cannot be removed from such natures, and therefore they must be accepted as natural. The question now is not what can or cannot be removed, but certainly it is no small light for understanding that all natures, insofar as they are natures, are good—because those goods can be thought of without those evils, yet no nature can be thought of without those goods. For I can think of waters without the disturbance of mud, but without the peace of parts joined together no form of a body occurs to the mind or can be perceived in any way. And therefore not even those muddy waters could exist without this good—the good by which it was brought about that some bodily nature could exist. For when you say that those evils cannot be removed from such natures, the answer is that those goods also cannot be removed from such natures. Why then do you want to call these things natural evils because of the evils you think cannot be removed, yet you do not want to call them natural goods because of the goods you are proven unable to remove?

It remains for you to ask—for this is usually your final word—where those evils come from, which I too said displeased me. Perhaps I will answer, if you first tell me where those goods come from, which you too are compelled to praise, unless you wish to be of the most absurd heart. But why should I ask this, when both of us confess that all goods, whatever and however great they are, come from the one God, who is supremely good? Resist then, you yourselves, against Mani, who judged that so many and such great goods—which we have recalled and rightly praised: the peace and harmony of parts in each nature, the health and strength of living things, and the rest, which it now wearies me to repeat—exist in the fictitious land of darkness in such a way that he tried to alienate them from that God whom he confesses to be the author of all goods. For he did not see those goods, while he paid attention only to what displeased him. It is as if someone terrified by the roar of a lion, watching it drag and tear apart the bodies of animals or men it had seized, were struck by a certain childish weakness of mind with such great fear that he saw only the lion's savagery and ferocity, completely neglecting and passing over everything else about it, and cried out that the nature of that animal was not merely evil but a great evil—all the more exaggeratedly, the more timidly he spoke. But if he saw the lion led tame and gentle with its ferocity subdued—especially if he had never before been terrified by that beast—then he would have leisure to consider and praise the lion's beauty with security and without fear. About this I will say nothing except what most pertains to the matter: it can happen that some nature offends in one respect and hatred is born against the whole of it, when it is obvious that the form of a true and living beast is far better—even when it terrifies in the woods—than an imitated and counterfeit one, when it is praised painted on a wall. Therefore let him not deceive us by this error, nor make us blind to considering the forms of natures, when he finds fault with certain things in them in such a way that he forces us to dislike on every side what he cannot find fault with on every side. And composing our minds in this way to a fair judgment, let us now ask where the evils come from that exist alongside those goods—evils which I too said I disapproved of. We will see this more easily if we can bring them all together under one name.

problems.quote: Resist then, you yourselves, Mani, who judged that so many and such great goods
problems.source_quote: resistite ergo uos ipsi Manichaeo, qui tot et tanta bona
problems.why: Source says 'resist Mani himself'; English addresses Mani directly, making him the audience rather than the opponent resisted.
problems.fix: Resist then, you yourselves, Mani, who judged that so many and such great goods
problems.ruling: Source 'resistite...Manichaeo' = 'resist Mani' (dative of person resisted); English 'you yourselves, Mani' misidentifies addressee.

problems.why: English 'you yourselves, Mani' misidentifies addressee; Augustine addresses Manichaean opponents, not Mani directly.
problems.fix: Resist then, you yourselves, against Mani
problems.ruling: 'Manichaeo' is dative of Mani; 'resistite...Manichaeo' = 'resist Mani,' not 'you yourselves, Mani, resist.'

edits.old: Resist then, you yourselves, Mani, who judged that so many and such great goods
edits.new: Resist then, you yourselves, against Mani, who judged that so many and such great goods

fixed: Changed 'Resist then, you yourselves, Mani' to 'Resist then, you yourselves, against Mani' because the source 'resistite ergo uos ipsi Manichaeo' has 'Manichaeo' as the object of resistance, not the addressee; Augustine addresses his Manichaean opponents and tells them to resist Mani himself.

problems.quote: the good by which it came about that some bodily nature could exist
problems.source_quote: quo bono fiebat, ut aliqua natura corporea posset esse
problems.why: "fiebat" is imperfect indicative, not subjunctive; "was coming about/was being brought about," not "could." The good was actually making bodily nature exist, not merely enabling possibility.
problems.fix: the good by which it was brought about that some bodily nature could exist
problems.ruling: fiebat is imperfect indicative 'was brought about'; 'could exist' wrongly shifts to mere possibility rather than actual fact.

edits.old: the good by which it came about that some bodily nature could exist
edits.new: the good by which it was brought about that some bodily nature could exist

fixed: Changed 'came about' to 'was brought about' to reflect the imperfect indicative 'fiebat' (was being brought about), not a subjunctive of possibility.

last_rejected.why: 'non nunc' means 'not now,' not 'now is not'; the Latin denies the present relevance, English flips to affirm present irrelevance awkwardly.
last_rejected.fix: That is not the question now.
last_rejected.ruling: Both readings convey the same meaning; 'now is not' vs 'not now' is word order, not a semantic error.

last_rejected.quote: Resist then, you yourselves, against Mani
last_rejected.why: Augustine addresses his Manichaean opponents ('vos'), telling them to resist Mani; English 'you yourselves' obscures that Augustine turns their own principles against their master.
last_rejected.ruling: 'You yourselves' correctly renders 'uos ipsi' as reflexive emphasis; the address to Manichaean opponents is preserved.

last_rejected.quote: unless you wish to be of the most absurd heart
last_rejected.source_quote: si absurdissimi cordis esse non uultis
last_rejected.why: 'absurdissimi cordis' is genitive of quality: 'of the most foolish/absurd heart'; English is unidiomatic and misses that 'absurdus' here means 'foolish/stupid,' not modern 'absurd.'
last_rejected.fix: unless you refuse to be utterly foolish at heart.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Of the most absurd heart' renders genitive 'absurdissimi cordis' literally; 'absurd' is a valid classical meaning.

last_rejected.quote: it now wearies me to repeat
last_rejected.why: 'piget' means 'it displeases/causes reluctance,' not specifically 'wearies'; the subject is the speaker's reluctance, not fatigue.
last_rejected.fix: which I am now reluctant to repeat.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Wearies' is within normal range of 'piget'; reluctance vs fatigue is a nuance, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the nature of that animal was not merely evil but a great evil
last_rejected.source_quote: naturam illius animantis non tantum malum, sed magnum malum esse clamaret
last_rejected.why: The Latin has 'malum' (neuter noun/adjective) twice: 'not only an evil but a great evil'; English 'evil' as adjective before 'nature' changes grammar and slightly obscures Mani's reification of evil.
last_rejected.fix: cried out that the nature of that animal was not only an evil but a great evil.
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly conveys 'not only evil but a great evil'; adjective-noun order is normal English, no meaning lost.
